Pope Leo cancels Assisi visit to focus on post-cancer surgery recovery

Pope Leo has canceled a planned October 27 visit to the Italian town of Assisi in order to avoid a helicopter flight as he recovers from a recent surgery for lung cancer.

Reuters

23 October, 2026 04:57 pm IST

VATICAN CITY, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Pope Leo has canceled a planned October 27 visit to the Italian town of Assisi in order to avoid a helicopter flight as he recovers from lung cancer surgery, the Vatican said on Friday.

The 71-year-old pontiff made the decision on doctors’ advice, the Vatican said, as a separate statement from his surgeon and personal doctor said a chest examination showed excellent progress in Leo’s recovery.

The pope had the lower lobe of his right lung removed in surgery on October 13 and was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Show Full Article

The pope’s doctors said on Wednesday that further exams of the tissue removed in the operation had confirmed the cancer was localized and he would not require any further ongoing cancer treatments.

Leo had been due to travel on October 27 to Assisi, about 175 km (109 miles) north of Rome, for a peace event with other religious leaders.

“To support his recovery following thoracic surgery last Tuesday, and in accordance with doctors’ advice, Pope Leo XIV will be unable to attend,” the Vatican statement said.

Leo was discharged from hospital on Saturday and is gradually resuming his normal duties. On Wednesday, he returned to St Peter’s Square for his weekly audience with pilgrims.

The Vatican has not said whether the pope will be able to go ahead with a scheduled November 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Reporting by Joshua McElwee, editing by Gavin Jones

HONG KONG, Oct 23 (Reuters) – China’s Commerce Ministry urged the United States on Friday to “respect the facts” and immediately end what it called discriminatory measures against Chinese research institutions.

The ministry also said in its statement that strengthening Chinese-US scientific research cooperation serves the common interest of both sides.

The comments were made in relation to the US Department of Defense putting US research funding restrictions on dozens of Chinese universities. A Republican lawmaker earlier this month called on the department to add 58 more Chinese schools and 62 Chinese technology labs to what is known as the 1286 list.

Show Full Article

Several of the Chinese labs and schools named by the lawmaker focus on areas such as semiconductors, AI and quantum computing, according to a letter reviewed by Reuters.

“The US’s actions are essentially coercing US research institutions to take sides, deliberately undermining normal China-US scientific research cooperation,” the Commerce Ministry said.

“This will only weaken the US’s own scientific and technological progress,” it said.

The Department of Defense, which US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth call the Department of War, is barred from providing research funding to any entity that works with Chinese universities on the list. The department says collaboration with schools on the list a compliance issue that puts US federal funding at risk.

(Reporting by Farah Master and the Beijing newsroom; Editing by Christopher Cushing and Tom Hogue)

From Buenos Aires to Colombo, discontent simmers under the surface of rebounding economies

Reuters

23 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Libby George, Nicolás Misculin and Uditha Jayasinghe LONDON/BUENOS AIRES/COLOMBO, Oct 23 (Reuters) – Gustavo Raul Perez furrows his brow over a notebook at the hardware shop he has run for six years on the outskirts of Buenos Aires.

Since Javier Milei became president of Argentina in 2023 — with Perez’s vote — rapid reforms have thrilled investors and won praise from the International Monetary Fund. Perez, though, mainly feels the pinch.

“This economic plan is for a few,” he said.

Show Full Article

Inflation has fallen to roughly 33% from nearly 300%, imports have opened up and subsidies have fallen.

But Perez’s restocking costs have tripled and customers have less to spend.

“There was a middle class three years ago,” he says. “It doesn’t exist anymore.”

Perez’s experience reflects a tension coursing through emerging economies: reforms that restored investor confidence and stabilised public finances have yet to improve living standards for many.

In Morocco, glittering new office towers contrast with frustration on city outskirts. In Sri Lanka, economic crisis and debt default have subsided but poverty remains above pre-crisis levels.

From fuel subsidy removal in Nigeria to privatisation in Egypt and market opening in Uzbekistan, years of reforms have helped emerging economies weather shocks — yet often grate with citizens who hear of economic turnarounds that do nothing for them.

Nigeria’s finance minister warned failing to address inequality is like “sitting on gunpowder”. Morocco’s central bank says stubborn unemployment has widened the gap between economic performance and citizens’ perceptions.

“When people in emerging markets are faced with rising food, fuel and energy costs…that is what they feel immediately,” says Torbjorn Soltvedt of Verisk Maplecroft, warning that unrest and instability could follow. Indeed, average global civil unrest risk hit its highest in nearly a decade this year, according to his company.

‘NO OTHER CHOICE’

The IMF and investors have long pressed emerging economies to reduce subsidies and currency controls.

The pandemic, then food and fuel spikes after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, jolted many into action: cutting spending, liberalising exchange rates and hiking interest rates.

Removing subsidies and weakening currencies raises prices even as spending cuts squeeze incomes — but leaders had “absolutely no other choice,” says Simon Quijano-Evans of Macro Hive, or they risk an “abyss” of lost investment.

The changes drew investors back; emerging economies now grow around 4%, roughly twice the pace of advanced economies.

But if public anger derails reform, these countries risk losing more than confidence — backsliding could stall the investment and job creation needed to narrow the gap with richer nations.

TWO-SPEED WORLD

In Morocco, foreign direct investment flow nearly doubled last year, but deadly youth-led protests rocked the country, and in July hundreds of would-be migrants flocked into a neighbouring Spanish enclave.

“Morocco is developing at two different speeds,” civil engineer Anass Sayad said while walking with his family in Casablanca Finance City. He pointed to stadiums and skyscrapers while saying that education and healthcare deserve more attention. The government boosted spending on both in its 2026 budget, though any impact will take time to reach its citizens.

The World Bank estimates 1.2 billion people in developing countries will reach working age over the next decade — raising doubts over whether investment will create enough jobs for them.

WORLDWIDE WORRY

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva warned higher fuel and food costs and declining development assistance were piling on pressure despite years of “hard work”, while the Fund called for more low-income country support.

Anger and unrest are not confined to emerging economies; cost-of-living pressures have brought protesters onto the streets of France, Italy and Spain.

But wealthy countries have greater fiscal firepower to cushion households. In developing economies inflation can also bite harder, with food accounting for 30% to 50% of consumer price baskets, compared with 13% to 14% in the US.

In Colombo, food vendor Sirimodara Wadaramge Sriyakanthi wakes before 5 a.m. to prepare herbal porridge and rice packets for lunch, absorbing higher costs to keep her prices near $2.

“I sell the lunch packets at a reasonable price so people can afford it,” she says, worrying about her son’s school fees and daughter’s dance lessons.

Sri Lanka may have emerged from crisis — but to her, little feels different.

“We have so many expenses,” she says.

($1 = 331.3500 Sri Lankan rupees)

(Additional reporting by Abdelhak Balhaki in Casablanca and Miguel Lo Bianco in Buenos Aires, editing by Karin Strohecker and Hugh Lawson)
